mayaya.title: Mayaya — From a personal idea to an essential tool
mayaya.description: AI bot capable of learning to play autonomously, providing statistics, a competition mode, and an in-game overlay
mayaya.subtitle: How a simple basic bot became the BombParty community’s favorite companion
mayaya.game_desc: BombParty is an online game where speed and vocabulary go hand in hand. Each round, a syllable appears (e.g., "tra"); players have a few seconds to type a word containing it ("travel", "contract", etc.) before the virtual bomb explodes. Easy to pick up, the real challenge lies in the pressure of the clock!

origin.title: Origin of Mayaya
origin.description: It all started with a simple observation: on BombParty, you couldn’t play solo or practice. No single-player mode, just public matches with random opponents. Frustrated by these limits (and admittedly a bit bored), I launched a little bot for fun

steps.title: A prank
steps.desc: Originally it was just a joke: a bot that replied 'feur' whenever someone typed 'quoi' in chat

steps.title: The .exe tool
steps.desc: The bot gained traction, so I added fun features. When a friend wanted to try it, I packaged everything into a Python app with a simple GUI

steps.title: Then the 24/7 bot
steps.desc: Running the bot locally was nice… but inconvenient. So I migrated to a Node.js bot hosted online around the clock, with over 30 commands and advanced training modes

steps.title: Finally, the overlay
steps.desc: The last hurdle was switching to chat to see scores and stats. So I added a visual overlay: a clean, responsive, modular interface

origin.conclusion: This journey—from simple prank to full overlay—inspired the BombParty devs to adopt many of these ideas natively!

funFact.title: Fun Fact: The war of attrition against Maca
funFact.intro: When I launched Mayaya, Maca—the BombParty staff’s enforcer—became a real blockade:

items.text: Only one bot was tolerated; all others were wiped out
Every 'fun' feature (profile GIFs, birthday alerts…) was removed in a hotfix
A stealth reCAPTCHA and WebSocket encryption to stifle any initiative

funFact.war_intro: Rather than giving up, we launched a real war of attrition:

warSteps.text: Bypassing the reCAPTCHA by simulating HTTP requests and user interactions
Intensive reverse-engineering of WebSocket traffic at every patch
Auto-adaptive scripts capable of keeping pace with real-time updates

funFact.conclusion: After a year-long tug-of-war against Maca (already widely despised by the community), he finally gave up. Before disappearing, he lifted all anti-bot protections (reCAPTCHA, obfuscation). A wave of innovative bots and new overlays swept in, and BombParty has never been more alive.

mayaya.remark_label: After two years of 24/7 operation, I stopped continuously hosting the bot due to lack of motivation to maintain the service. Other newer bots have emerged and taken up the torch, but the code remains available for local use.

arie.title: Arie — Personal Multifunction Discord Bot
arie.description: Discord bot offering a wide range of features: engaging mini-games, music streaming, customizable alerts, data storage, and much more
arie.subtitle: One single bot to replace an entire army of bots on our Discord server
arie.discord_desc: Discord is a free chat platform (voice, video, and text) extremely popular with gaming communities, students, and project teams. Each space is called a server, composed of text and voice channels. Discord bots are automated accounts capable of responding to commands and enriching the user experience (games, moderation, music, etc.).

origin.title: Origin of Arie
origin.description: Within our Discord server, the proliferation of specialized bots (music, mini-games, GPT, giveaways, etc.) became unmanageable: tedious maintenance, scattered permissions, and frequent outages (e.g., music bots relying on YouTube getting blocked). So we created Arie, guided by three principles:

steps.title: Centralization
steps.desc: Gather all truly useful features into a single bot.

steps.title: Customization
steps.desc: Offer a tailor-made experience (GPT personalities, inside-joke commands, etc.).

steps.title: Reliability
steps.desc: Ensure 24/7 availability and a polished UX (slash commands + buttons).

snapscore.title: SnapScore+ — Local multi-account orchestration
snapscore.description: Local multi-account orchestrator based on Node.js and Puppeteer. It drives multiple Chrome profiles to send and open snaps in loops using dedicated macros.
snapscore.subtitle: Automate the web interface to raise a Snap Score from a single machine

snapchat.title: About Snapchat
snapchat.description: Snapchat is a social network centered on sending ephemeral photos and videos. Snap Score increases by repeating two simple actions:
snapchat.context: With manual use, most accounts stay in the hundreds or a few thousand points. Reaching the millions is rare.

origin.title: Project origin
origin.intro: I wanted to measure how far a Snap Score could go by automating the interface like a human would, on a single machine and without servers.

steps.title: Mobile prototype
steps.desc: Two phones with simple macros establish a baseline of ~30 points/min. Enough to validate the idea and show that multiplying devices doesn’t scale.

steps.title: Web userscript
steps.desc: A Tampermonkey script that clicks through the web UI proves feasibility and doubles throughput to ~60 points/min, but the computer must stay focused on visible windows.

steps.title: Node.js/Puppeteer orchestrator
steps.desc: Multi-window control (dual main session plus assistants) with locks, short pauses and restart rules: the desktop remains usable while climbing to ~460 points/min across nine windows.

origin.focus: The orchestrator changes everything: it coordinates visibility, prevents collisions and recovers automatically.

architecture.title: Technical architecture
architecture.objective: Maximize the main account’s score by coordinating helper accounts locally, keeping steady throughput without remote infrastructure.
components: Local orchestrator (Node.js + Puppeteer) that opens, drives and supervises each window.
Main account split across two parallel windows to maximize useful sends.
Assistant accounts dedicated to opening snaps and feeding the backlog.
A scheduler that assigns roles, paces sends/reads and monitors session health.
resourceManagement: Camera lock: only one send at a time on the main account.
Controlled backlog: automatic pause beyond 25 unread snaps to drain the queue.
Threshold restarts: a window is restarted when send/read latency exceeds ~1 s, which brings reads back to ~500 ms and sends to ~700 ms after reset.
Visibility guardrails: every action waits for the targeted element to exist and be visible, faster on average and without arbitrary timers.
observability: Per-window counters: successful sends/reads, queue size, and p50/p95 latencies.
startCheckingIssues loop: aggregates averages, computes points/min and triggers targeted restarts (main, assistants or global).
Structured logs (startLog) with session duration, send/read averages, backlog and blocked/healthy states.
Automatic slowdowns or restarts as soon as p95 drifts.
stack: Initial prototype as a Tampermonkey userscript

mobile.label: Mobile prototype
mobile.objective: Validate the idea: sync one phone that sends and another that opens to measure the real gain.
advantages: Close to normal app usage, so very low risk.
limits: Multiple phones plugged in continuously.
Camera and apps unavailable during the session.
Finicky macro tuning.

web.label: Web userscript
web.objective: Speed up cleanly: automate through the browser to chain sends/reads while keeping live visibility.
advantages: Clear settings, fast tests, easy iterations.
Browser tools help understand and fix quickly.
limits: PC monopolized without a second screen.
Any Snapchat UI change breaks the automation.
Platform defenses: throttling, dropped sessions.
Camera and mic monopolized by the browser, possible conflicts.
On long sessions: slowdowns and growing memory.

puppeteer.label: Puppeteer orchestrator
puppeteer.objective: Maximize score: run multiple accounts in parallel on one machine with simple rules, priorities and continuous monitoring.
advantages: Each account isolated with automatic reconnection.
Windows visible or hidden, scheduled launches and regular checks.
Fine-grained resource control: who gets the camera, when to restart, how to avoid bottlenecks.
Centralized monitoring with clear indicators updated every second.
Can be deployed on other machines if needed.
limits: Performance depends on hardware: CPU, RAM, disk, video encoding.
Memory grows with the number of instances.
puppeteer.perf: ~430 points/min on my setup with 2 main accounts and 7 assistants

observation.title: Findings before the final version
items: A Snapchat account can be connected in two places at the same time.
Leaving a session open too long ends up slowing everyone down.
The camera can’t be used by two instances simultaneously.
observation.conclusion: These findings guided the rules: limit session duration, queue camera access and restart as soon as metrics drift.

management.title: Instance management
items: An AccountManager supervises the accounts: connection, health checks and role assignment.
Each account has its own browser profile with saved cookies to reconnect automatically.
Main accounts send snaps, assistants open them.

monitoring.title: Continuous monitoring
items: Each window directly watches its conversation to act at the right moment, without arbitrary timers.
Aggregated counters track sends, reads, averages and backlog size in real time.
These metrics refresh in the console every 500 ms to keep tight control of the system.

rules.title: Resource rules
items: Camera lock: only one account has camera access at a time.
Controlled queue: pause as soon as more than 25 snaps remain unread.
Targeted restarts when send or open averages drift.
Auto-reconnect: if a window closes or numbers go off the rails, cut and relaunch cleanly.

learnings.title: What this demonstrates

A well-tuned local orchestrator is enough to manage multiple accounts without remote infrastructure.
Simple rules like the camera lock, backlog limit and latency guard make the system predictable and easy to fix.

ariesmod.title: Magic Garden Ecosystem
ariesmod.description: An ecosystem of seven projects around the game Magic Garden: mod, community hub, public API that extracts the game's data, backend, Android app and maintenance driven by AI agents. Nearly 40,000 players.
ariesmod.subtitle: Seven projects built around one game: a mod, a community hub, a public API, an Android app and maintenance driven by AI agents. Nearly 40,000 players.

game.title: About Magic Garden
game.description: Magic Garden is a multiplayer idle game available on Discord and magicgarden.gg. The concept: buy seeds, grow plants, sell them and get richer over time. Mechanics like pets (offering bonuses), weather (influencing prices) and multiplayer (up to 6 players, with sell bonuses based on room size) add depth to what seems like a childish game at first glance.

origin.title: Project Origin
origin.headline: From a Discord night to a community mod
origin.intro: It all started during a Discord evening with friends. We stumbled upon this game by accident, and honestly, my first reaction was: "It's childish, the gameplay really isn't great." But very quickly, an idea crossed my mind.

steps.title: The discovery
steps.desc: "OK the game sucks, but can't I just try to become the richest player?" My developer instinct kicked in instantly.

steps.title: Reverse engineering
steps.desc: I started dissecting the game: reading the minified JavaScript bundle, analyzing network requests, breaking down every WebSocket message. The goal, understand every mechanism to figure out what I could exploit.

steps.title: The first mod
steps.desc: I built a first mod focused on automation to accumulate money quickly and posted it on the game's public Discord. No rules, no security, the game had only been out for two months.

steps.title: Meeting the devs
steps.desc: A game developer reached out to me. Supportive, he said he was happy someone was taking interest in his game this early, but that this type of mod wasn't allowed. And that's when I saw another opportunity.

steps.title: The real beginning
steps.desc: What if, instead of automating, I created a community mod that players actually need? A mod that enhances the experience without breaking the game. That's where the real project started, systematically asking for dev approval before every feature.

origin.conclusion: This transparent approach built a trust relationship with the developers that allowed the project to grow for months.

api.label: API & Garden Explorer
api.objective: The game keeps the list of its plants, its pets and their prices to itself. This project goes and fetches that list on its own, and makes it available to anyone.
api.story_intro: At first I copied that list into the mod by hand. As long as the game barely changed, it held up.

story_steps.title: The chore
story_steps.desc: Every game update changed a price or added a plant, and the whole list had to be redone by hand. I was spending more time copying than building.

story_steps.title: The realisation
story_steps.desc: The game obviously knows its own plants and prices, otherwise it could not put them on screen. Rather than copying that list, I could teach a program to go and read it by itself.

story_steps.title: The bet
story_steps.desc: The catch is that the game does not lay this information out to be found easily, and it moves it around with every new version. The bet was that automatic reading would find its way anyway. Since then it has absorbed over 300 versions of the game without me touching it.

story_steps.title: Garden Explorer
story_steps.desc: Once all that information was available, all it lacked was a shop window. That is where Garden Explorer came from: a site where any player can look up plants, pets and their prices, with nothing to install.

optimization_rules: Cache invalidated by game version change, not by timer
Concurrent requests on an empty cache deduplicated: only one does the work
ETag and 304 responses for clients already up to date
Stale data served immediately, recomputed in the background
Sprites and static files served by Nginx, without waking Node
Poller realigned onto the game's deadlines rather than a fixed interval
Composed-image cache capped, evicting the oldest entries
k6 load tests: tiers, latency thresholds, SSE stream capacity
features: All game data over REST: plants, seeds, crops, pets, eggs, items, decor, mutations, abilities and weather
Live shops and weather, fed by a permanent connection to the game server
Composed images on demand: a pet with its variant and mutation, generated then cached
Historical statistics: how often items show up in shops, weather history
Interactive Swagger documentation, testable straight from the browser
Weather forecast, 100% accurate over the last 24 hours (287 out of 287)
CSV and TSV exports that import straight into Google Sheets
Garden Explorer: a public site to follow live shops and weather, browse the history, game data and animations, and use the calculators with nothing to install
Adapts to game updates on its own, with no manual work
limits: Tied to the game's internal structure: if the data format changes deeply, the extraction has to be adapted by hand
A single server, with no redundancy and no automatic failover
The history has gaps whenever the service stops, since nothing backfills what was missed
Unofficial API: no agreement with the game's developers, it could stop working overnight

client.objective: Create a Tampermonkey mod that enriches the Magic Garden experience without breaking the game, adding community features and quality-of-life improvements that players are asking for.
client.story_intro: The mod evolved over months, each feature added in response to community needs and validated by the game developers.

story_steps.title: The foundations
story_steps.desc: First official version with the most requested features from the community. The mod was immediately adopted by players.

story_steps.title: The takeoff
story_steps.desc: The game had no public room system, yet playing with more people increases sell prices. I created a Discord bot coupled with the game's API to list available rooms directly in the mod. This is when the mod really took off.

story_steps.title: Editor mode
story_steps.desc: An idea that surprised everyone, developers included. A purely visual mode, but one that dramatically boosted the community aspect of the game.

story_steps.title: Constant maintenance
story_steps.desc: The game was being updated constantly. Multiple mod updates per week, sometimes per day. Core systems were rebuilt several times: sprite system, game data system, Discord compatibility.

hub.label: Community Hub
hub.objective: The game's social hub, pulled out of Aries Mod to stand on its own: friends, messages, groups, public rooms, leaderboards, and a game of chess playable in the garden.
hub.story_intro: The hub was born inside Aries Mod, as one feature among many. Except it grew faster than everything else, and plenty of players were installing a full game overlay for it alone.

story_steps.title: A product inside the product
story_steps.desc: The hub had its own screens, its own server, its own settings, and users who wanted nothing to do with the rest of the mod. You had to install a full game overlay just to message a friend. The feature had outgrown its box.

story_steps.title: The extraction
story_steps.desc: So the hub was released on its own, installable by itself. For anyone already using it inside Aries Mod there was nothing to redo, it picks up their login and their settings automatically.

hub.chess_title: A game of chess in the garden
hub.chess_intro: The idea came from a plain observation: players already spent hours waiting around in the garden with nothing to do together. What was missing was a game inside the game, something two people at the same spot could do without depending on the game itself.
chess_points: The engine handles every rule: legal moves, castling, en passant, promotion, check, checkmate and stalemate. It is verified by a perft, the standard method for validating a move generator, which counts every position reachable to a given depth and compares against the published totals. 33 test cases, including a count of 4,865,609 positions at depth 5: one badly generated move anywhere and the total stops matching

The rendering is not a board laid on top of the game. These are the real garden tiles, the real sprites and the real sounds: the board is built inside the game world, and pieces move on click or by drag and drop
hub.chess_outro: A game of chess inside a gardening game, played on real vegetable-patch tiles. It is the most useless thing I have ever written, and by far the one that demanded the most precision.
features: Friends and online status, with a look at a friend's garden and inventory even outside their room
Private and group messaging
Groups of up to 100 members, with moderation tools
Public rooms: over 150 rooms listed and kept alive by the community
Leaderboards and badges
Profiles with seven independent privacy settings
Multiplayer chess playable right in the garden
Works both in the browser and in the Discord Activity
Installable alone or alongside Aries Mod, with no conflict between the two
limits: Depends on the backend and on Discord: without either, the social features are down
Two transports to maintain in parallel: SSE on the web, long polling in the Discord Activity
Two mods to keep alive at once, with every shared change needing testing on both sides
An account is required for anything social, which rules out players unwilling to link their Discord

backend.label: Backend (VPS)
backend.objective: Provide a lightweight, low-cost infrastructure for the mod's community features: rooms, real-time chat, friends, groups and leaderboards. It now knows nearly 40,000 players.
backend.story_intro: The backend came out of necessity. When the game's public rooms API was pulled after abuse, I rebuilt the feature myself, with the mod's own players as the data providers.

story_steps.title: The Supabase phase
story_steps.desc: I had planned for 50 users at most, and the free tier of 500,000 requests a month was going to be plenty. One hour after release I already had my 50 users. Within 24 hours there were 400. In under a week the quota was gone.

story_steps.title: Moving to a VPS
story_steps.desc: Moved onto a Hetzner VPS in two days, at €3.6 a month, for a theoretical capacity of 20 million requests a day. Completely disproportionate, and exactly what was needed.

story_steps.title: The Community Hub
story_steps.desc: With over 1,000 users, the most glaring gap was social. I built the Community Hub on this backend, and it ended up becoming a project in its own right. It has its own tab.

story_steps.title: Security and compatibility
story_steps.desc: Discord OAuth to secure sign-in. Real-time events did not get through inside Discord, so I backed the system with a second way of delivering them. A week of non-stop work to make it run everywhere.

story_steps.title: The optimisation
story_steps.desc: With 10,000 registered players and 500 connected at once, the VPS was running at 200% capacity for 5 million requests a day. After a heavy rebuild it came back down to 900,000 requests a day and 25% load. Still on the same €3.6 server.

story_steps.title: Ko-fi and supporters
story_steps.desc: I added a Ko-fi page without expecting much. €50 in the first week, and over a hundred euros across the first month, enough to cover more than two years of hosting. I added Supporter badges to the Community Hub to thank contributors.

features: Public room system fed directly by mod players
Full Community Hub: real-time chat, friends, groups, leaderboard, real-time view of friends' garden, inventory and pets without being in their room
Secure authentication via Discord OAuth
Long polling with event system (workaround for Discord restrictions)
Admin console with Discord login, read-only SQL console and supervision of the AI maintenance
Massive optimization: from 5M to 900K requests/day, VPS at 25% capacity
limits: Two transports to maintain in parallel: SSE on the web, long polling in the Discord Activity where event streams do not get through
Single VPS without redundancy
Dependency on Discord OAuth for authentication

    messageRateLimit.ts  # Message rate limiting

Dockerfile  # Multi-stage Docker build
optimization_rules: In-memory TTL cache (30s) for global data (rooms, leaderboard, online players)
PostgreSQL-backed rate limiting per IP and per player, with IP blocklist
Long polling with waiter pattern: server holds request until an event arrives or timeout
Unified fan-out: a single push serves both SSE and long-polling consumers
Parallel aggregation: 11 queries via Promise.all for initial data load
Lazy presence sweep: timer only runs when players are connected
Recipient deduplication for presence events (friends + group members)
Bulk upserts for room players (single INSERT instead of N)
Partial and composite PostgreSQL indexes targeting frequent queries
Lazy room cleanup (cleanup-on-read, no cron needed)

android.label: Android app
android.objective: In Magic Garden you have to leave the game open to keep earning your bonuses. This app takes over from your phone, using almost nothing, at any hour and wherever you are.
android.story_intro: Magic Garden rewards those who stay connected. Except staying connected, in practice, means leaving your computer running.

story_steps.title: A computer running for nothing
story_steps.desc: To avoid losing bonuses you had to keep the game open at all times. Overnight while you sleep, during the day while you are at school or at work. A computer running for hours purely so the garden keeps moving.

story_steps.title: The phone takes over
story_steps.desc: The idea fit in one sentence. Let the phone hold the seat instead of the computer. But for anyone to leave it running day and night, the app had to cost almost nothing. No game running in the background, no images reloading over and over, just one line kept open to the game's server. The bare minimum needed to keep the bonuses coming.

story_steps.title: The phone that shuts everything down
story_steps.desc: Except a phone spends its life saving battery. Screen off, the app got cut. Phone asleep, it vanished. Swiped from the recent apps list, it never came back. It had to be taught to survive the system. These days it does not drop anymore.

story_steps.title: Playing without opening the game
story_steps.desc: Once the connection held, it would have been a waste to stop there. Planting, watering, harvesting, buying, feeding pets, selling crops. Almost everything you do in Magic Garden can be done from the app, and when you actually want to play, one button opens the real game with the mod already in place.

android.structure:
app/src/main/java/com/mgafk/app/
  auth/                # Discord login
  data/
    websocket/         # Game connection and protocol
    websocket/state/   # Game state models
    repository/        # Sessions and state reporting
    model/
  service/             # Background service and watchdog
  play/                # Opening the game inside the app
  ui/screens/          # Garden, pets, shops, alerts, social
  ui/components/
features: Connection held in the background, screen off and app closed
Live tracking of pets, garden, shops and weather
Alerts configurable per section or per item, with a loud alarm mode
Remote actions: plant, water, harvest, buy, feed, sell
Up to 30 saved pet teams
Several accounts in parallel, managed through tabs
A button to open the real game inside the app, with the mod already injected
Local image cache, so sprites are not re-downloaded on every screen
limits: The workarounds depend on Android policy: a new system version can break whatever keeps the app alive
No automatic session renewal, you have to sign in again by hand when the token expires
Android only, no iOS version
Some manufacturers are far more aggressive about sleep than others, so behaviour varies from phone to phone

gemini.label: Gemini
gemini.objective: Starting over with another developer to build the definitive mod: able to absorb the game's updates on its own, working across every browser and on mobile, and easy for someone else to pick up.
gemini.story_intro: After months on Aries Mod, the limits of the original architecture were becoming obvious. Another developer and I decided to start over from scratch. The mod is now shipped and in service.

story_steps.title: The collaboration
story_steps.desc: Another developer was also playing the game and had his own mod. We decided to merge our two projects into one, starting from scratch with an architecture built to last.

story_steps.title: The architecture
story_steps.desc: Documented strict rules, a modular architecture with clear layers (atoms, globals, modules, features, UI), and a clean separation of concerns. No more hardcoded game data, everything is dynamically extracted.

story_steps.title: Compatibility
story_steps.desc: All-browser compatible from day one, mobile optimized, and designed so any developer can fork and add their own sections easily.

story_steps.title: Claude as copilot
story_steps.desc: The project architecture is largely managed with Claude. Workflows, rules, and skills are defined in the .claude directory, enabling much smarter and cleaner coding. Every contribution automatically follows these guidelines.

gemini.structure:
src/
  api/  # Public API (window.Gemini)
  atoms/  # Bridge to the game's Jotai store
  globals/  # Reactive derived variables
  modules/  # Game modules (Data, Sprite, Pixi, Audio...)
  features/  # 20+ independent features
  websocket/  # Capture and transport
  ui/  # Interface (Shadow DOM, components, sections)
  utils/  # Cross-cutting utilities
  main.ts  # Entry point
features: Modular architecture with documented strict rules
Auto-adaptation to game structure (no more hardcoded data)
All-browser compatible + mobile optimized
20+ independently toggleable features
Public API exposed (window.Gemini) for third-party scripts
Dynamic sprite system via MGSprite and data via MGData
limits: A more demanding architecture, with a learning curve for contributors
Still tied to the game bundle, whose structure can change deeply

maintenance.label: AI maintenance
maintenance.objective: The game ships several versions a day, and any of them can break the API or the mods. This system watches, triages bugs and prepares fixes with AI agents. All I have left to do is review and approve.
maintenance.story_intro: With nine projects all depending on the same game, I spent my evenings fixing whatever the latest update had broken. I automated the repetitive part and kept the final decision.

story_steps.title: Watching
story_steps.desc: Every five minutes, a script asks the game for its version, which costs 18 bytes. On each new version, it checks every API endpoint and compares the shape of each response, never its content: otherwise the changing weather would raise a permanent alert.

story_steps.title: Learning to stay quiet
story_steps.desc: In the first nights, the same message came in 119 times before morning, and an alert fired whenever the game added an item. I taught the system to check again a minute later before alerting, and to report only what actually breaks. Monitoring is only worth something if it is rare.

story_steps.title: Autonomous repair
story_steps.desc: When an endpoint breaks for a new reason, a Claude agent looks for the cause in the game's code and fixes the API. It has no git and no network: the loop restarts the API, checks again and rolls back if anything is still broken. On the test bench, the right fix came in 148 seconds.

story_steps.title: Player bug reports
story_steps.desc: Players report bugs from inside the mod, in their own language. A fast model matches the message to the right feature using a map of the code, an agent diagnoses in read-only mode, then writes a fix only if a test reproduces the bug first. 27 of the first 34 reports were fixed.

story_steps.title: The supervisor
story_steps.desc: Everything is driven from the backend's admin console. There I talk with a supervisor that sees incidents, open problems and one agent per project, through an MCP server I wrote without any library. Nothing ships or reaches a player without my click.

maintenance.structure:
src/
  detector/      # Watches the API and game versions
  autonome/      # Autonomous repair with rollback
  signalements/  # Bug triage, diagnosis, fix and delivery
  superviseur/   # Console conversation and MCP server
  commun/        # Heavy-job lock, activity log, backend client
  config/        # Registry of tracked projects
  scripts/       # Cron jobs and map generators
agents/          # One profile per tracked project (9 projects)
data/            # API fingerprints, catalogs, code maps
optimization_rules: Nothing is pushed, released or sent to a player without my click
Repair only on a new failure, at most 3 attempts a day
The repair model has no git, no PM2 and no network: the loop restarts, checks and restores
A full outage (stopped process, Nginx) is never handed to the model, it is not a code bug
Player text is treated as data, never as instructions (prompt injection defense)
A fix is only written once a test reproduces the bug
One heavy job at a time on the machine, enforced by a lock on disk
The supervisor runs without built-in tools (no files, commands or web), only its MCP tools
No agent starts below 900 MB of free memory, so the production API never slows down
features: API monitoring every 5 minutes, full check on each game version
Incidents opened and closed automatically in the admin console
Snapshot of the game's catalogs on each version, to spot new content and changed fields
Autonomous API repair with restart, re-check and rollback
Player reports understood in several languages and grouped when they describe the same problem
Diagnosis in an isolated copy of the repository (git worktree), tested fix, one-click delivery
Automated Android delivery: branch, CI, reading test results, tag
Conversational supervisor with about 25 MCP tools and one agent per tracked project
limits: A diagnosis takes several minutes, longer than a human who already knows the code
Everything runs on the same small server as the API: free memory limits parallel jobs
The mods are not monitored automatically, they get fixed from player reports
Depends on the Claude CLI: if it is no longer signed in, monitoring goes on but diagnoses and repairs wait

items.text: ~700 daily users on Arie's Mod alone
~800,000 requests a day, on a €3.60/month VPS running the whole ecosystem
~20,000 downloads of the releases published on GitHub
Over €100 raised on Ko-fi in one month, enough to cover more than two years of hosting
Compatible with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera GX and Discord Activities

learnings.title: What this project demonstrates
items: Reverse engineering is a powerful tool when used constructively and transparently
Underestimating your user base is the best mistake you can make, it forces you to learn scaling under real conditions
A well-configured €3.6/month VPS can outperform €25/month cloud solutions
Community trust is built through transparency and asking for permission rather than forgiveness
User feedback is the best fuel for a developer

items.text: MG Answer Bot: a Python bot that answers players' questions citing its sources (game API, wiki) and refuses to answer without evidence. RAG with embeddings and Claude, evaluated on real questions, 347 tests.

Contribution to Starweaver-API, the shared API of the game's mod authors: 48 typed WebSocket functions, a guide and tests written before the code. Pull request merged in May 2026, and I co-administer the modders' GitHub organization.
MG-Websocket-Helper: a Node.js client that rebuilds the full game state like the official client (JSON Patch), the foundation of the Android app.
Telegram shop alert bot in English, French and Russian, built on the API.

frida.title: Frida IL2CPP Toolkit
frida.subtitle: A toolkit to observe and modify Unity games while they run, drivable by hand or by an AI.
frida.description: A TypeScript toolkit for instrumenting compiled Unity games. Chained tools, an agent that stays attached to the game, and a local server that lets an AI drive the exploration in real time.

about.title: About Unity
about.description: Unity is the engine a large share of games are built with, from small mobile titles to major releases. When a studio ships one, it can compile it using a technique called IL2CPP: the code is translated into machine language, the kind a processor runs directly. The game gets faster, but it becomes unreadable. Class and function names are gone, so is the structure, and all that remains is a program running with no manual.
about.frida: Frida is the tool that hands control back. It attaches to an already running program, reads its memory and intercepts its functions while it works. The game no longer has to be readable on disk, you only have to watch it live. Everything in this project rests on that.

origin.title: How it started
origin.intro: I have always had a foot in game modding. But there was one door I kept stopping in front of.

steps.title: The wall
steps.desc: Games compiled with IL2CPP were out of reach. You open the file and there is nothing to read. I knew what I wanted to do, I just had no way in.

steps.title: Depending on no one
steps.desc: There were ready-made frameworks for writing mods. They worked, but they meant building on someone else's tool and never understanding what happened underneath. I wanted the opposite.

steps.title: The toolkit
steps.desc: Frida broke the deadlock. My first attempts were throwaway scripts, and every new question meant starting over. I ended up gathering the moves that kept coming back into tools that chain together, sitting on an agent that stays attached to the game.

steps.title: Letting an AI drive
steps.desc: What was left was opening the tool to something other than a keyboard. I added a local server that exposes that agent behind a single address. An AI can now explore the game while it runs, ask for a class, install an interception, read what comes out and decide the next move on its own. Reverse engineering becomes a conversation with the game.

workflow.title: The six-tool workflow
workflow.intro: Each tool answers one question, and its answer feeds the next. That sequence is what turns an opaque binary into something you can work with.

steps.title: 1. Analyse
steps.desc: What does this game contain? An inventory of the loaded libraries, the available classes, the active components.

steps.title: 2. Find a class
steps.desc: Where are the player, the inventory, the game manager? The search works even when the names have been made unreadable.

steps.title: 3. Catch a live object
steps.desc: Grab a real instance in memory and read every one of its fields. This is where you discover what the game actually handles.

steps.title: 4. Follow the calls
steps.desc: Intercept a method and record what goes in and what comes out, on every call. This is what reveals the game's logic.

steps.title: 5. Modify
steps.desc: Change a value live, without restarting the game. The test loop is measured in seconds.

steps.title: 6. Invoke
steps.desc: Trigger one of the game's own methods on demand, as if the game had called it itself.

frida.structure:
src/
  lib/           # Briques reutilisables importees par les outils
    search.ts      # Recherche de classe, meme sans nom lisible
    instances.ts   # Capture d'objets vivants en memoire
    dump.ts        # Lecture de tous les champs d'un objet
    hook.ts        # Interception des appels de methode
    patch.ts       # Modification de valeurs en direct
    invoke.ts      # Appel d'une methode du jeu a la demande
  tools/         # Un fichier = un outil autonome
  presets/       # Configuration par jeu cible
app/
  backend/       # Serveur local qui heberge la session Frida
    routes/        # Une porte d'entree unique, plus les routes metier
    core/
      labels/        # Noms donnes aux classes obfusquees
      annotations/   # Notes attachees aux decouvertes
      migrations/    # Report des noms d'une version du jeu a l'autre
  frontend/      # Interface locale pour explorer a la main
features: Analysis of a running game, with no need to decompile it first
Class lookup by name, including when the name has been deliberately obscured
Capture of a live object in memory and a read of all its fields
Interception of a method's calls, with incoming and outgoing values
Live value changes and on-demand invocation of the game's own methods
A persistent agent: the session stays open, the game is never restarted between two questions
A local server exposing that agent behind a single address, so an AI can drive it in real time
A live event stream, pushed from the game to the client as execution goes on
Recovered names kept from one game version to the next, carried over automatically after an update
A local interface to explore by hand whenever you would rather drive yourself
limits: Tied to the target's internal structure, which changes with every game update
Limited to Unity games compiled with IL2CPP
The server is meant to run locally only, it has no protection for being exposed
Still an ongoing project, the tools evolve with each new target

dofus.title: Dofus, the proving ground
dofus.description: Dofus is a protected game, with obfuscation and names deliberately made unreadable. It was the worst possible case, which made it the right test. The toolkit found its way through regardless, and every name recovered there is recorded then carried over automatically to the game's next version. That is what convinced me it held up: if the tool gets through a target built to stop it, it will get through the rest.

learnings.title: What this project shows
items: Turning down the ready-made solution costs time up front, and pays back in understanding forever.
A compiled binary is not a black box, it is a running program you can question.
Obfuscation slows you down, it does not stop you. Searching by structure rather than by name is enough to get around it.
Putting a tool behind one simple entry point makes it drivable by something other than yourself, an AI included.
Splitting a skill into composable tools beats one big script: every piece will serve again on the next target.
